El programa de Hilbert no fue una ingenu: Hilbert's programme was no naivety: it was the reasonable answer to a real crisis. Russell's paradox — the set of all sets that do not contain themselves — had blown naive set theory apart in 1901, and firm ground was needed. Gödel proved that absolutely firm ground does not exist, but the conclusion should not be overstated: mathematics went on working exactly the same the next day. What was lost was not reliability, but the aspiration to a mechanical and definitive guarantee. And out of the ruins came something enormous: to prove that there is no method that decides everything, Turing had to define precisely what a method is, and in that definition is the computer.
El resultado de Turing es, literalmente,: Turing's result is, literally, the birth certificate of computer science. The 1936 paper was not about building machines: it was about proving a negative theorem. But along the way it defines the universal machine — a machine able to simulate any other by reading its description from the tape — which is exactly the idea of the stored-program computer: a device whose behaviour is not in the hardware but in data supplied to it. Everything you run today is a particular case of that construction, invented to prove that something was impossible.

Un siglo antes que Turing, <strong>Ada L: A century before Turing, Ada Lovelace had already thought about what a computing machine can and cannot do. In 1843 she translated a paper on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was never built, and added notes three times longer than the original. In them she described step by step how the machine would compute the Bernoulli numbers, which is considered the first published program, and she sensed that it could manipulate any symbol, not only numbers, and even compose music. She also wrote that the machine could not “originate” anything, only do what it was ordered to; in 1950, Turing devoted a section of his most famous paper to discussing the “Lady Lovelace objection”.
